chunks: "Say the load current steps up by two amps.
At that instant the inductor current hasn't changed, because an inductor resists current changes: it can only ramp at V in minus V out over L.
So the extra two amps have to come from the output capacitor.
First there's an immediate step from the capacitor's ESR, I times ESR, and a bit from its ESL, and then the capacitor voltage starts to droop at delta I over C.
The feedback loop sees the output drop. After some delay from the sensing and the error amplifier, it increases the duty cycle, perhaps all the way to its maximum.
The inductor sees a larger voltage across it and ramps up, in my example at 1. 85 amps per microsecond, so it takes a little over a microsecond to get from one amp to three.
The droop bottoms out when the inductor current crosses the new load current, because then the capacitor stops discharging.
But the inductor current has to overshoot the load current for a while to put back the charge the capacitor lost.
Then the loop pulls the duty cycle back down and the output settles. How much it rings depends on the phase margin.
The release is the reverse: the inductor has excess current, which dumps into the capacitor, and the output overshoots.
It's usually the harder case at low output voltages, because the inductor current only falls at V out over L, which is slow."
